methodological_rigor.justification: The study integrates 29 cohorts (n=8,886) with a clearly defined pipeline for identifying ESLs (10% least variable CpGs in 1,658 healthy young adults) and a reproducibility-oriented threshold (99.9th percentile across three independent control cohorts). An a priori power calculation using powerSurvEpi is reported for the cardiogenic shock sub-cohort (n=64, 85% power, HR=1.5), and survival models adjust for age, sex, clonal hematopoiesis status, and 12 immune cell fractions. Permutation testing (1,000 iterations) with Bonferroni correction supports the diagnosis-relapse pairing claim, and the methods explicitly state no randomization/blinding because the study is retrospective associative. Limitations include heavy reliance on secondary GEO datasets with heterogeneous platforms, median splits for DMI (which can bias effect estimates), and absence of external validation for the Framingham-derived DMI thresholds; sensitivity analyses are limited to quartile re-analysis.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is primarily a retrospective observational analysis combining multiple cohort datasets (Framingham Heart Study offspring Exam 8, cardiogenic shock cohort, pan-hematological cancer compilations), with longitudinal AML sampling—most consistent with Oxford 2b for the prognostic analyses. Clinical relevance is high: findings propose a blood-based epigenetic biomarker (DMI) that complements genetic CH testing for leukemia monitoring, residual-disease assessment in mutation-negative patients, and cardiovascular risk stratification (HR 1.57 for CHD; HR 3.76 in cardiogenic shock after adjustment). Endpoints include patient-relevant outcomes (overall mortality, CVD, CHD, CHF). Translation remains a step away from clinical implementation—no prospective validation, no analytic/clinical validity work for an assay, and effect sizes modest in the general cohort—so relevance stops short of practice-changing.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the most applicable standard given the multi-cohort observational prognostic design (REMARK partially applies to the biomarker-DMI analyses). The methods detail cohort composition (Supplementary Data 1), preprocessing (minfi, Noob, probe filters), inclusion/exclusion for Framingham (prior endpoints excluded), sex-and-gender considerations, and reference a Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary. Numerous GEO accessions (GSE40279, GSE87571, GSE115278, GSE197676, GSE124413, GSE132203, GSE141682) and external resources (TCGA, GTEx, JASPAR, scATAC datasets) are named; a Source Data file is referenced. Omissions include lack of an a priori analysis plan/pre-registration, no formal participant-flow diagram across the amalgamated cohorts, limited reporting of missing data handling, and reliance on Supplementary Data for key cohort characteristics.

novelty_literature.justification: The study introduces a conceptually novel framework—defining a stable epigenetic baseline (ESLs) in healthy young blood and operationalizing deviation as a single-sample metric (DMI)—and applies it across hematological malignancies, aging, and cardiovascular disease. It extends prior DNAm-outlier work (Teschendorff et al. in breast/cervical pre-neoplasia; Gentilini on stochastic epimutations) by (i) deriving a blood-specific stable reference, (ii) linking lineage-biased perturbation to progenitor chromatin accessibility, and (iii) connecting the metric to cardiovascular outcomes beyond epigenetic clocks. The integration with scATAC lineage specificity and the demonstration of persistent epigenetic memory from diagnosis to relapse are meaningful empirical advances. It is not first-in-class—stochastic epimutation and outlier-methylation concepts predate it—so this is a strong extension rather than a paradigm shift.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with a clear narrative arc from ESL definition → cancer perturbation → clonal memory → aging → cardiovascular risk → mechanism, and the abstract is quantitatively grounded (31,744 ESLs, 8,886 individuals, 29 cohorts). Figures and captions are informative and standalone-interpretable, with explicit statistical annotations (HRs, P-values, test identities). Acronyms (ESL, DMI, CH, CGI, TSS) are defined on first use; the discussion appropriately separates driver-vs-passenger interpretations. Minor issues include dense methods paragraphs that could be subsectioned further, occasional verbose discussion of mechanism without new data, and the Statistics subsection stating 'Python version 3.1.1' which is almost certainly a typo for 3.11.1.

key_strengths: Novel conceptual framework (ESLs/DMI) with a clearly defined, reproducible derivation pipeline and threshold set from three independent control cohorts
Large-scale integration across 29 cohorts and 8,886 individuals spanning hematological malignancies, aging, and cardiovascular outcomes
Convergent biological validation: lineage-biased perturbation matched to progenitor chromatin accessibility via two independent scATAC datasets, plus TF-motif/5mC-SELEX mechanistic linkage

Prospective-style analytic rigor where feasible: a priori power calculation for the cardiogenic shock sub-cohort, Cox models adjusted for age/sex/CH status/immune cell fractions, Bonferroni correction, and permutation testing for diagnosis-relapse pairing
Patient-relevant endpoints (all-cause mortality, CVD, CHD, CHF) with Framingham follow-up up to 14 years; demonstration that DMI remains prognostic independent of DNMT3A/TET2 CH
key_concerns: Observational, retrospective design with reliance on secondary GEO datasets limits causal inference and introduces platform/batch heterogeneity despite 450K/EPIC harmonization
No prospective or external validation of DMI thresholds or clinical cutpoints; median-split dichotomization can inflate effect estimates and limit clinical translation
Reporting lacks explicit pre-registration/analysis plan, a consolidated STROBE/REMARK checklist, and a cross-cohort participant-flow diagram
Mechanistic claims about TF-motif disruption and gene silencing are correlative; functional perturbation experiments (e.g., targeted methylation at RGS2 or KLF12 targets) are not performed
Cardiogenic shock sub-cohort (n=64) is modest and intentionally underpowered for CH comparisons; broader generalizability of the HR=3.76 effect requires replication
Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'Python version 3.1.1' typo; dense Methods subsections) and incomplete discussion of missing-data handling
chief_reviewer.rationale: A conceptually novel, methodologically solid, large-scale observational study with convergent biological evidence and plausible translational implications; falls short of tier-1 practice-changing status due to retrospective design, lack of prospective validation, and primarily correlative mechanism, placing it at the top of tier 2 with minor revisions.
